children: Dear Reader,

The Panorama newsletter is sent to Moneycontrol Pro subscribers on market days. It offers easy access to stories published on Moneycontrol Pro and gives a little extra by setting out a context or an event or trend that investors should keep track of.
What is common between the uber rich of the world and Indian households? Physical gold.

Gold has grabbed headlines for obvious reasons in recent months. There is a war going on which is just one of the many crises that are in progress globally right now and the time-tested protection for human beings has been to store wealth in physical gold. The thinking behind buying and stashing gold is the belief that bullion offers protection against everything, from inflation to total societal collapse.

This interesting FT article, free to read for Moneycontrol Pro subscribers, explains how gold storing infrastructure has seen an unprecedented demand. A global race to build underground vaults is on to meet the demand from the wealthy who want to stash gold worth millions of dollars.
But why are the rich loading up on physical gold now? There is a whole platter of reasons available, but only one matters and that is fear.

The wealthy are opting to keep their gold on the shelf instead of in bytes on a computer. This speaks to the liquidity and accessibility of their wealth in dire times. Of course, behind this fear is the force of other factors which include the dollar debasement trade.

The US Treasury’s move to double its buyback plan has dragged the dollar down. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent may have ordered this size upgrade to tell the bond market that it is driving up yields unnecessarily, but all he achieved was to bring the market’s focus on the US government’s mighty debt pile. At a time when there are clear signs of foreign investors’ reluctance to keep buying US treasuries, reminding the market of an unsustainable pile of debt is a wrong move. Enter gold as the old candidate that promises to safeguard investors from the world’s largest reserve currency. Add the US-Iran war’s impact on supply chains, AI’s assault on employment and other events that have all jacked up uncertainty, and the case for gold is as untarnished as the metal itself.

That brings us to the magnet that attracts investors to the metal: its price. Globally gold prices have doubled in just a year in dollar terms and the rally that stumbled a little is back again. Despite being down 17 percent since January’s highs, gold still fetches a higher value than it did a year ago.

While the wealthy have begun stashing physical gold anew, Indian households are old hands in this business. Obsessed with physical gold for centuries, households here are perhaps changing their approach and are now leveraging their gold holdings. Jefferies estimates that households hold 25,000 tonnes of physical gold, which was worth $3.9 trillion as of March this year. Gold loans have grown 73 percent over the past two years and are now 7 percent of total bank and non-bank credit, points out Jefferies. The brokerage estimates that 15 percent of total household gold holdings is now monetised through such loans.

Experts have pointed out that the attitude towards gold is changing and it is increasingly being seen as an asset to be monetised to meet other demands in life. Gold buying in India is cultural, which is why it is unlikely that physical gold purchases will ease even if prices remain elevated. The upcoming festival season will likely mirror earlier ones and become a gold buying spree.

An odd but understandable development is the entry of organised large gold jewellery chains such as Titan and Kalyan Jewellers in the cash for gold segment. A practice so far seen only in small gold shops in the unorganised sector is now being adopted by almost every gold retailer. They are now offering to buy back household gold and give cash instead of exchanging the same for gold jewellery. This has to do with the pressure on margins for such retailers as gold prices continue to rise.
Gold’s eternal sunshine works for investors, from the uber rich to the poor household. What it harms is the profit margins of retailers and India’s current account position.

The uber wealthy’s run after physical gold seldom impacts the current account of the country to which they belong but Indian households’ obsession with the metal is costing the country its current account strength. Is it a price worth paying every year?
